title: A Dirty Word or a Dirty World?
abstract: We explored the effect of attribute framing on choice, labeling charges for environmental costs as either an earmarked tax or an offset. Eight hundred ninety-eight Americans chose between otherwise identical products or services, where one option included a surcharge for emitted carbon dioxide. The cost framing changed preferences for self-identified Republicans and Independents, but did not affect Democrats' preferences. We explain this interaction by means of query theory and show that attribute framing can change the order in which internal queries supporting one or another option are posed. The effect of attribute labeling on query order is shown to depend on the representations of either taxes or offsets held by people with different political affiliations.

claims.text: Labeling environmental surcharges as either an earmarked tax or an offset changes choice preferences for self-identified Republicans and Independents.
Labeling environmental surcharges as either an earmarked tax or an offset does not affect the preferences of self-identified Democrats.
Attribute framing changes the order in which decision-makers pose internal queries supporting alternative options.
The effect of attribute labeling on internal query order depends on the mental representations of taxes or offsets held by individuals with different political affiliations.

methodologies.name: Attribute framing choice experiment with query theory analysis
methodologies.description: Participants made choices between products or services featuring a carbon dioxide surcharge framed either as a tax or an offset, with query theory used to trace the order of internal decision queries.
